title: Part 5, Chapter 1
paragraphs: The morning after the fateful confrontation with Dounia and her mother had a sobering effect on Pyotr Petrovitch. As deeply unpleasant as it was, he was gradually forced to accept as an irreversible fact what had seemed fantastic and unbelievable just the day before. The black snake of wounded vanity had been gnawing at his heart all night. When he got out of bed, Pyotr Petrovitch immediately looked in the mirror. He was afraid he might have jaundice. But his health seemed unimpaired so far, and looking at his noble, fair-skinned face, which had grown somewhat plump lately, Pyotr Petrovitch was briefly comforted by the conviction that he could find another bride -- perhaps even a better one. But returning to reality, he turned aside and spat vigorously, which drew a sarcastic smile from Andrey Semyonovitch Lebeziatnikov, the young friend he was staying with. Pyotr Petrovitch noticed that smile and immediately chalked it up against his young friend. He had been keeping quite a tally of late. His anger doubled when he realized he should never have told Andrey Semyonovitch about the outcome of yesterday's meeting. That was the second mistake he had made in a fit of temper and impulsiveness. Moreover, all morning one annoyance followed another. He even ran into a snag with his legal case at the senate. He was particularly irritated by the landlord of the apartment he had rented in anticipation of his wedding and was having redecorated at his own expense. The landlord, a wealthy German tradesman, refused to consider breaking the freshly signed lease and demanded the full penalty payment, even though Pyotr Petrovitch was returning the place practically renovated. Likewise, the furniture shop refused to return a single ruble of the deposit for items purchased but not yet delivered.

"Am I really to get married just for the sake of the furniture?" Pyotr Petrovitch ground his teeth, and at the same time a flash of desperate hope crossed his mind. "Can it really be so irrevocably over? Is there no point in making one more attempt?" The thought of Dounia sent a sharp pang of desire through his heart. He suffered real anguish at that moment, and if it had been possible to kill Raskolnikov by sheer force of will, Pyotr Petrovitch would have done so on the spot.

"It was my mistake not to have given them money," he thought, making his way gloomily back to Lebeziatnikov's room. "Why on earth was I so stingy? It was false economy! I meant to keep them penniless so they'd turn to me as their savior, and look what happened! If I'd spent fifteen hundred rubles on trousseau and gifts -- trinkets, dressing cases, jewelry, fabrics, all that rubbish from Knopp's and the English shop -- my position would have been stronger. They couldn't have refused me so easily! They're the sort of people who would feel obligated to return money and gifts if they broke it off, and they'd find it hard to do so! Their conscience would prick them: how can we dismiss a man who has been so generous and considerate? I've made a blunder."
And grinding his teeth again, Pyotr Petrovitch called himself a fool -- though not aloud, of course.

He returned home twice as irritated and angry as before. The preparations for the funeral dinner at Katerina Ivanovna's caught his attention as he passed through. He had heard about it the day before; he even had a vague memory of being invited, but he'd been too absorbed in his own troubles to pay attention. Inquiring of Madame Lippevechsel, who was busy laying the table while Katerina Ivanovna was away at the cemetery, he learned that the event was to be quite an affair. All the lodgers had been invited, including some who hadn't known the dead man, and even Andrey Semyonovitch Lebeziatnikov had been invited despite his previous quarrel with Katerina Ivanovna. He, Pyotr Petrovitch, was not only invited but eagerly expected as the most distinguished of the lodgers. Amalia Ivanovna herself had been invited with great ceremony despite the recent unpleasantness, and she was very busy with preparations, taking obvious pleasure in them. She was dressed to the nines in new black silk and was proud of it. All this gave Pyotr Petrovitch an idea, and he went into his room -- or rather Lebeziatnikov's -- somewhat thoughtfully. He had learned that Raskolnikov was to be one of the guests.

Andrey Semyonovitch had been at home all morning. Pyotr Petrovitch's attitude toward this man was strange, though perhaps natural. He had despised and hated him from the day he moved in, and at the same time seemed somewhat afraid of him. He hadn't come to stay with him in Petersburg simply out of cheapness, though that had been perhaps his main reason. He had heard of Andrey Semyonovitch, who had once been his ward, as a prominent young progressive who played an important role in certain notorious circles whose activities were legendary in the provinces. This had impressed Pyotr Petrovitch. These powerful, all-knowing circles that despised everyone and exposed everyone had long filled him with a peculiar but vague dread. He couldn't, of course, form even an approximate idea of what they actually stood for. Like everyone else, he had heard there were progressives of some sort in Petersburg -- nihilists and the like -- and, like many people, he exaggerated and distorted the meaning of those words to an absurd degree. What he had feared most for many years was being exposed, and this was the chief source of his constant anxiety about moving his affairs to Petersburg. He was frightened of this the way small children are sometimes seized by panic. Some years back, when he was just starting his career, he had encountered two cases in which rather important provincial figures, his patrons, had been cruelly exposed. One case had ended in a great scandal for the person attacked, and the other had very nearly ended in serious trouble. For this reason, Pyotr Petrovitch intended to look into the matter as soon as he reached Petersburg and, if necessary, to get ahead of things by courting favor with "the younger generation." He relied on Andrey Semyonovitch for this, and before his visit to Raskolnikov he had managed to pick up some fashionable phrases. He soon discovered that Andrey Semyonovitch was a commonplace simpleton, but that by no means reassured him. Even if he could be certain that all the progressives were fools like him, it wouldn't have calmed his nerves. He had no real interest in any of the doctrines, ideas, or systems that Andrey Semyonovitch pestered him with. He had his own agenda -- he simply wanted to find out what was happening here. Did these people have any power or not? Did he have anything to fear from them? Would they expose any of his dealings? And what exactly were they going after now? Could he somehow win them over if they really were powerful? Was that the thing to do? In short, hundreds of questions presented themselves.

Andrey Semyonovitch was an anemic, scrofulous little man with strangely flaxen mutton-chop whiskers he was very proud of. He was a clerk and almost always had something wrong with his eyes. He was rather soft-hearted but self-assured, and sometimes extremely pompous in his speech -- which had an absurd effect coming from such a small man. He was one of the lodgers most respected by Amalia Ivanovna, because he didn't get drunk and paid his rent on time. Andrey Semyonovitch really was rather stupid. He had attached himself to the cause of progress and "the younger generation" out of sheer enthusiasm. He was one of that numerous and varied legion of mediocrities, half-formed creatures, and conceited half-educated coxcombs who latch onto whatever idea happens to be most fashionable, only to vulgarize it and turn into a caricature every cause they serve, however sincerely.

Despite his good nature, Lebeziatnikov was also beginning to dislike Pyotr Petrovitch. This happened on both sides without either realizing it. Simple as Andrey Semyonovitch was, he had begun to see that Pyotr Petrovitch was using him and secretly despising him, and that "he was not the right sort of man." He had tried expounding the systems of Fourier and Darwin to him, but lately Pyotr Petrovitch had begun listening too sarcastically and even rudely. The fact was that Pyotr Petrovitch had started to suspect that Lebeziatnikov was not merely a commonplace simpleton but perhaps a liar too, and that he had no connections of any consequence even in his own circles, but had simply picked up ideas thirdhand. Very likely he didn't even know much about his own propaganda work, because he was too muddled. A fine person to expose anyone! It should be noted, by the way, that during those ten days Pyotr Petrovitch had eagerly accepted the strangest flattery from Andrey Semyonovitch. He hadn't objected, for instance, when Andrey Semyonovitch praised him for being ready to contribute to a new "commune," or for agreeing not to christen his future children, or for consenting if Dounia took a lover a month after the wedding. Pyotr Petrovitch so enjoyed having his virtues extolled that he didn't disdain even these when they were attributed to him.

That morning Pyotr Petrovitch had cashed some five-percent bonds, and now he sat at the table counting bundles of banknotes. Andrey Semyonovitch, who almost never had any money, paced the room pretending to regard all those banknotes with indifference and even contempt. Nothing could have convinced Pyotr Petrovitch that Andrey Semyonovitch could really look at the money unmoved, while the latter kept thinking bitterly that Pyotr Petrovitch was perfectly capable of believing this about him and was perhaps even glad of the chance to tease his young friend by reminding him of his inferiority and the vast difference between them.

He found Pyotr Petrovitch incredibly inattentive and irritable that morning, though he, Andrey Semyonovitch, had launched into his favorite subject -- the founding of a special new "commune." The brief remarks that escaped from Pyotr Petrovitch between the clicking of beads on the counting frame betrayed unmistakable and discourteous irony. But the "humane" Andrey Semyonovitch attributed Pyotr Petrovitch's foul mood to his recent break with Dounia, and he was burning with impatience to hold forth on this topic. He had something progressive to say that would console his worthy friend and "could not fail" to advance his development.
"There's some kind of celebration being prepared at that widow's, isn't there?" Pyotr Petrovitch asked suddenly, interrupting Andrey Semyonovitch at the most interesting point.
"Don't you know? I was telling you about it last night, what I think of all such ceremonies. And she invited you too, I heard. You were talking to her yesterday..."

"I never would have expected that penniless fool to spend all the money she got from that other fool Raskolnikov on this feast. I was amazed just now, passing through, at the preparations -- the wines! Quite a few people are invited. It's beyond belief!" continued Pyotr Petrovitch, who seemed to have some purpose in pursuing the conversation. "What? You say I was invited too? When was that? I don't remember. But I won't go. Why should I? I only mentioned to her in passing yesterday the possibility of her obtaining a year's salary as the destitute widow of a civil servant. I suppose she invited me on that account, eh? Ha-ha-ha!"
"I don't intend to go either," said Lebeziatnikov.
"I should think not, after giving her a beating! You might well think twice, ha-ha!"
"Who beat whom?" cried Lebeziatnikov, flustered and blushing.

"You beat Katerina Ivanovna about a month ago. I heard about it yesterday. So that's what your convictions amount to... and the women's rights question wasn't quite sound either, ha-ha-ha!" And Pyotr Petrovitch, as though comforted, went back to clicking his counting beads.

"That's all slander and nonsense!" cried Lebeziatnikov, who was always sensitive about this subject. "It wasn't like that at all, it was completely different. You've heard it wrong -- it's a lie. I was simply defending myself. She came at me first with her nails, she pulled out my entire whiskers. I hope any person has the right to defend himself. I never allow anyone to use violence against me on principle, because it's an act of tyranny. What was I supposed to do? I simply pushed her away."
"Ha-ha-ha!" Luzhin went on laughing spitefully.

"You keep on like that because you're in a bad mood yourself. But that's nonsense and has nothing, absolutely nothing to do with the women's question! You don't understand. I used to think that if women are equal to men in all respects, even in physical strength -- as some now maintain -- then there should be equality in that too. Of course, I realized afterward that such a question really shouldn't arise, because there shouldn't be any fighting, and in the future society fighting is unthinkable. And it would be absurd to seek equality in fighting. I'm not that stupid. Though of course there is fighting now -- there won't be later, but for now there is -- damn it! You get me all confused! It's not because of that that I'm not going. I'm not going on principle, so as not to participate in the revolting convention of memorial dinners -- that's why! Though of course one might go just to laugh at it. A pity there won't be any priests -- I'd certainly go if there were."
"So you'd sit down at someone else's table and insult both it and your hosts, is that it?"

"Certainly not insult -- protest. I'd do it with a worthy purpose. I might indirectly serve the cause of enlightenment and propaganda. It's the duty of every person to work for enlightenment and propaganda, and the more harshly the better, perhaps. I might plant a seed, an idea. Something might grow from that seed. How would I be insulting them? They might be offended at first, but afterward they'd see I'd done them a service. You know, Terebyeva -- who's in the commune now -- was criticized because when she left her family and gave herself to... her cause, she wrote to her father and mother saying she refused to go on living conventionally and was entering a free marriage. People said it was too harsh, that she should have been gentler in her letter. I think that's all nonsense -- there's no need for softness. On the contrary, what's needed is protest. Varents had been married seven years. She left her two children and wrote her husband a straightforward letter: 'I've realized I cannot be happy with you. I can never forgive you for hiding from me that another form of social organization exists through communities. I only recently learned of this from a great-hearted man to whom I have given myself, and with whom I am establishing a community. I speak plainly because I consider it dishonest to deceive you. Do as you see fit. Don't hope to win me back -- it's too late. I hope you will be happy.' That's how such letters should be written!"
"Is that the Terebyeva you said had entered a third free marriage?"

"No, it's only the second, actually! But what if it were the fourth, or the fifteenth -- that's all nonsense! And if I ever regretted the death of my father and mother, it's now. Sometimes I think: if my parents were still alive, what a protest I could have aimed at them! I would have done something deliberate -- shown them, astonished them! I really do wish there were someone to rebel against!"
"To astonish! Ha-ha! Well, have it your way," Pyotr Petrovitch interrupted. "But tell me this: do you know the dead man's daughter, the delicate little one? Is what they say about her true?"

"What of it? In my personal conviction, this is the normal condition of women. Why not? That is -- let me be precise. In our present society it's not altogether normal because it's forced upon them, but in the future society it will be perfectly normal because it will be voluntary. Even as things stand, she was entirely within her rights. She was suffering, and that was her asset, so to speak -- her capital, which she had every right to use as she saw fit. In the future society there will of course be no need for such assets, but her role will have a different significance -- rational and in harmony with her surroundings. As for Sofya Semyonovna personally, I regard her actions as a bold protest against the organization of society, and I deeply respect her for it. I actually rejoice when I look at her!"
"I heard you got her thrown out of these lodgings."
Lebeziatnikov was furious.

"That's more slander!" he yelled. "It wasn't like that at all! That was all Katerina Ivanovna's invention -- she didn't understand! And I never made advances to Sofya Semyonovna! I was simply developing her, entirely unselfishly, trying to awaken her sense of protest. All I wanted was her protest, and besides, Sofya Semyonovna couldn't have stayed here anyway!"
"Have you asked her to join your commune?"

"You keep laughing, and very inappropriately, if you don't mind my saying so. You don't understand! There's no such role in a commune. The commune exists precisely so that there should be no such roles. In a commune, such a role is fundamentally transformed -- what is degrading here becomes perfectly sensible there; what is unnatural under present conditions becomes completely natural in a commune. It all depends on the environment. Everything is environment, and the individual is nothing. And I'm on good terms with Sofya Semyonovna to this day, which proves she never felt wronged by me. I'm trying to draw her into the commune now, but on an entirely different basis. What are you laughing at? We're trying to establish our own commune, a special one, on a broader foundation. We've gone further in our convictions. We reject more! And meanwhile I'm continuing to develop Sofya Semyonovna. She has a wonderful, wonderful character!"
"And you take advantage of her fine character, do you? Ha-ha!"
"No, no! Quite the opposite."
"The opposite! Ha-ha-ha! What a thing to say!"
"Believe me! Why would I hide it? In fact, I find it strange myself how timid, chaste, and modest she is with me!"
"And you, of course, are developing her... ha-ha! Trying to prove to her that all that modesty is nonsense?"

"Not at all! How crudely, how stupidly -- forgive me -- you misunderstand the word development! Good heavens, how crude you still are! We're striving for the freedom of women, and all you can think of is one thing. Setting aside the general question of chastity and feminine modesty as useless in themselves and indeed mere prejudices, I fully accept her chastity toward me, because that's her choice to make. Of course, if she herself were to tell me she wanted me, I'd consider myself very fortunate, because I like the girl very much. But for now, no one has ever treated her more courteously than I have, with more respect for her dignity. I wait in hope -- that's all!"
"You'd do better to give her a present. I bet that never occurred to you."

"You don't understand, as I've already told you! Of course she's in that situation, but it's a different question entirely. You simply look down on her. Observing a fact that you wrongly consider worthy of contempt, you refuse to take a humane view of another person. You don't know what a character she has! I'm only sorry that lately she's completely stopped reading and borrowing books. I used to lend her mine. I'm also sorry that despite all her energy and determination in protest -- which she's already demonstrated once -- she has so little independence, so little self-reliance, so as to break free from certain prejudices and foolish notions. Yet she understands some questions very well -- for instance, about hand-kissing: that it's an insult to a woman for a man to kiss her hand, because it implies inequality. We had a debate about that, and I described it to her. She also listened attentively to an account of French workers' associations. Right now I'm explaining the question of entering another person's room in the future society."
"And what's that about?"
"We had a debate recently on the question: does a member of the commune have the right to enter another member's room, man or woman, at any time? And we decided: yes, they do!"
"And what if it's an awkward moment? Ha-ha!"
Lebeziatnikov was genuinely annoyed.

"You always think of something indecent," he cried with disgust. "How frustrated I am that when I was explaining our system, I brought up the question of personal privacy too soon! It's always a stumbling block for people like you -- they turn it into a joke before they understand it. And how pleased with themselves they are! I've always maintained that this question shouldn't be tackled by a beginner until he has firm faith in the system. And tell me, please, what do you find so shameful about cesspools? I'd be the first to volunteer to clean out any cesspool you like. It's not about self-sacrifice -- it's simply work, honorable and useful work, as good as any other and far better than the work of a Raphael or a Pushkin, because it's more useful."
"And more honorable, more honorable! Ha-ha-ha!"

"What do you mean by 'more honorable'? I don't understand such terms when applied to human activity. 'More honorable,' 'nobler' -- those are outdated prejudices that I reject. Everything that is useful to humanity is honorable. I understand only one word: useful! You can snicker all you like, but that's how it is."

Pyotr Petrovitch laughed heartily. He had finished counting the money and was putting it away. But some of the banknotes he left on the table. The "cesspool question" had already been a subject of dispute between them. What was absurd was that it genuinely angered Lebeziatnikov, while it amused Luzhin -- and at that moment he particularly wanted to irritate his young friend.

"It's yesterday's bad luck that makes you so ill-humored and annoying," Lebeziatnikov blurted out. Despite his "independence" and "protests," he still didn't dare stand up to Pyotr Petrovitch and continued to treat him with something of the old deference.

"You'd better tell me this," Pyotr Petrovitch interrupted with haughty displeasure. "Can you -- or rather, are you really on friendly enough terms with that young woman to ask her to step in here for a moment? I think they've all come back from the cemetery. I heard the sound of footsteps. I want to see her, that young woman."
"What for?" Lebeziatnikov asked in surprise.

"I have my reasons. I'm leaving here today or tomorrow, and there's something I wanted to discuss with her. But you may be present during the conversation. In fact, it would be better if you were. Otherwise, God knows what you might imagine."
"I won't imagine anything. I was only asking. If you have something to say to her, nothing could be easier than to call her in. I'll go right now, and you can be sure I won't be in your way."

Five minutes later Lebeziatnikov returned with Sonia. She came in looking very surprised and overcome with her usual shyness. She was always awkward in such situations and always afraid of new people -- she had been that way as a child, and was even more so now. Pyotr Petrovitch greeted her "politely and warmly," but with a certain tone of teasing familiarity which he considered appropriate for a man of his standing when dealing with a creature so young and so interesting as she. He hastened to "put her at ease" and seated her at the table facing him. Sonia sat down, looked around -- at Lebeziatnikov, at the banknotes lying on the table, then back at Pyotr Petrovitch -- and her eyes remained fixed on him. Lebeziatnikov moved toward the door. Pyotr Petrovitch motioned for Sonia to stay seated and stopped Lebeziatnikov.
"Is Raskolnikov in there? Has he arrived?" he asked in a whisper.
"Raskolnikov? Yes. Why? Yes, he's there. I saw him come in just now. Why?"

"Well, I particularly ask you to stay here with us and not leave me alone with this... young woman. I only want a few words with her, but God knows what people might make of it. I wouldn't want Raskolnikov to spread stories. You understand what I mean?"

"I understand!" Lebeziatnikov saw the point. "Yes, you're right. Of course, I'm personally convinced you have no reason to worry, but... still, you're right. Certainly I'll stay. I'll stand by the window and won't be in your way. I think you're right."

Pyotr Petrovitch returned to the sofa, sat down opposite Sonia, looked at her closely, and assumed an extremely dignified, even severe expression, as if to say: "Don't get any ideas, young lady." Sonia was overwhelmed with embarrassment.

"First of all, Sofya Semyonovna, please make my apologies to your respected mother. That is the right way to put it, isn't it? Katerina Ivanovna is like a mother to you?" Pyotr Petrovitch began with great dignity, though affably.
His intentions were clearly friendly.
"Yes, exactly -- like a mother," Sonia answered timidly and hurriedly.
"Then please convey my apologies to her. Due to unavoidable circumstances, I'm forced to be absent and won't be attending the dinner despite your mother's kind invitation."
"Yes... I'll tell her... right away."
And Sonia jumped hastily to her feet.

"Wait, that's not all," Pyotr Petrovitch stopped her, smiling at her simplicity and ignorance of good manners. "You know me poorly, my dear Sofya Semyonovna, if you think I would trouble a person like you over something so trivial, concerning only myself. I have another purpose."

Sonia sat back down quickly. Her eyes flickered again for an instant to the gray-and-rainbow-colored banknotes still on the table, but she quickly looked away and fixed her gaze on Pyotr Petrovitch. She felt it horribly inappropriate, especially for someone like her, to stare at another person's money. She glanced at the gold eyeglass Pyotr Petrovitch held in his left hand and at the massive, extremely handsome ring with a yellow stone on his middle finger. But then she looked away again and, not knowing where to turn, ended up staring straight at Pyotr Petrovitch's face once more. After a pause of even greater solemnity, he continued.
"Yesterday in passing, I happened to exchange a few words with Katerina Ivanovna, poor woman. That was enough for me to determine that she is in a condition that is -- how shall I say -- abnormal."
"Yes... abnormal," Sonia agreed hurriedly.
"Or to put it more simply and clearly: she's ill."
"Yes, more simply and clearly... yes, ill."

"Quite so. And therefore, from a feeling of humanity and -- so to speak -- compassion, I would be glad to help her in any way I can, given her unfortunate position. I believe this entire destitute family now depends entirely on you?"
"May I ask," Sonia said, rising to her feet, "did you say something to her yesterday about the possibility of a pension? Because she told me you had promised to get her one. Is that true?"

"Not in the slightest -- it's absurd! I merely hinted at the possibility of temporary assistance as the widow of a civil servant who had died in the service -- provided she had connections. But apparently your late father hadn't served his full term and hadn't even been in active service recently. In fact, even if there were any hope, it would be extremely slim, because there would be no real claim for aid -- quite the opposite. And she's already dreaming of a pension! Ha-ha-ha! Quite a go-getter, that woman!"

"Yes, she is. She's trusting and good-hearted, and she believes everything because of the goodness of her heart, and... and she's like that... Yes. Please excuse her," said Sonia, and again she stood up to go.
"But you haven't heard what I have to say."
"No, I haven't," murmured Sonia.
"Then sit down." She was dreadfully flustered; she sat down again for the third time.

"Given her situation with her unfortunate little ones, I would be glad, as I've said, to be of service to the extent that I can -- that is, to the extent of my ability, and no more. One might, for instance, organize a subscription for her, or a lottery, something of that sort -- the kind of thing that's always arranged in such cases by friends or even strangers who wish to help. That was what I meant to discuss with you. It could be done."
"Yes, yes... God will reward you for it," Sonia whispered, gazing intently at Pyotr Petrovitch.

"It could be done, but we'll discuss it later. We might begin today -- we'll talk it over this evening and lay the groundwork, so to speak. Come to see me at seven o'clock. Mr. Lebeziatnikov, I hope, will help us. But there is one thing I must warn you about in advance, and it's the reason I've asked you here, Sofya Semyonovna. In my opinion, it would be impossible -- indeed, unsafe -- to put money directly in Katerina Ivanovna's hands. Today's dinner is proof of that. She doesn't have so much as a crust of bread for tomorrow, or a decent pair of shoes, and yet she's bought Jamaica rum, even Madeira I think, and coffee. I saw it as I passed through. Tomorrow you'll all be back to having nothing. It's absurd. So it seems to me that the subscription money should be managed so that the unfortunate widow doesn't know about it -- and that only you, for instance, should handle it. Am I right?"

"I don't know... it's only today, just this once. She was so set on honoring him, on celebrating his memory. And she is very sensible, really... but whatever you think best, and I'd be very, very... they'll all be... and God will reward... and the orphans..."
Sonia burst into tears.

"Very well then, keep it in mind. And now, would you accept this small sum for your relative's benefit, from me personally? I'm very anxious that my name not be mentioned in connection with it. Here... having my own concerns, so to speak, I cannot do more."

And Pyotr Petrovitch held out to Sonia a ten-ruble note, carefully unfolded. Sonia took it, blushed crimson, jumped up, muttered something, and began to take her leave. Pyotr Petrovitch escorted her ceremoniously to the door. She escaped from the room at last, agitated and distressed, and returned to Katerina Ivanovna overwhelmed with confusion.

All this time Lebeziatnikov had been standing by the window or pacing the room, trying not to interrupt the conversation. When Sonia left, he walked up to Pyotr Petrovitch and solemnly held out his hand.

"I heard and saw everything," he said, emphasizing the last word. "That was honorable -- what I mean is, it was humane! You wanted to avoid her gratitude, I could see that! And though I cannot, I confess, sympathize in principle with private charity -- because it not only fails to eliminate evil but actually promotes it -- I must admit that I witnessed your action with pleasure. Yes, yes, I approve."
"That's all nonsense," muttered Pyotr Petrovitch, somewhat disconcerted, looking carefully at Lebeziatnikov.

"No, it's not nonsense! A man who has suffered the distress and humiliation you went through yesterday, and who can still feel for others' misery -- such a man, even if he is making a social error, still deserves respect! I honestly didn't expect it of you, Pyotr Petrovitch, especially given your views. Oh, what a hindrance your views are to you! How upset you are, for instance, by yesterday's bad luck," cried the warmhearted Lebeziatnikov, feeling a renewed surge of affection for Pyotr Petrovitch. "And what do you need with marriage, with legal marriage, my dear, noble Pyotr Petrovitch? Why do you cling to this legality of marriage? You can beat me if you want, but I'm glad -- genuinely glad -- it fell through, that you're free, that you're not entirely lost to humanity! You see, I've spoken my mind!"
"Because I don't want to be made a fool of in your free marriage and raise another man's children -- that's why I prefer legal marriage," Luzhin replied, just to say something.
He seemed preoccupied with something.

"Children? You mentioned children," Lebeziatnikov began like a warhorse at the sound of a trumpet. "Children are a social question of the first importance, I agree, but the question of children has another solution. Some people refuse to have children altogether because they represent the institution of the family. We'll discuss children later, but now, the question of honor -- that's my weak point, I confess. That hateful, militaristic, Pushkin-era word is unthinkable in the vocabulary of the future. What does it even mean? Nonsense! There will be no deception in a free marriage! It's simply a natural consequence of legal marriage, its corrective, so to speak -- a protest. So it's not humiliating at all. And if I ever -- to suppose the absurd -- were legally married, I'd actually be pleased. I'd say to my wife: 'My dear, until now I loved you. Now I respect you, because you've shown you can protest!' You laugh! That's because you can't break free of prejudices. Damn it all! I understand what's unpleasant about being deceived in a legal marriage, but that's simply a despicable consequence of a despicable situation in which both parties are degraded. When the deception is open, as in a free marriage, it ceases to exist -- it's inconceivable. Your wife would simply be proving how much she respects you by considering you incapable of opposing her happiness and avenging yourself on her for her new partner. Damn it all! Sometimes I daydream: if I were to marry -- legally or otherwise, it's all the same -- I'd present my wife with a lover if she hadn't found one herself. 'My dear,' I'd say, 'I love you, but even more than that, I want your respect. See!' Am I not right?"

Pyotr Petrovitch sniggered as he listened, but without much amusement. He was barely listening. He was preoccupied with something else entirely, and even Lebeziatnikov eventually noticed it. Pyotr Petrovitch seemed agitated and kept rubbing his hands. Lebeziatnikov remembered all this and reflected on it afterward.
